title: Whether the personal subsistence of the Logos is communicated to his human nature; and whether they speak rightly who say Christ's humanity subsists everywhere by that subsistence
pass_a_gloss: Article XII. Whether personal subsistence of the Logos is communicated to his human nature; whether they speak rightly who say Christ's humanity subsists everywhere by the Logos's subsistence, and exists everywhere according to its personal being. Para1 From the common saying that the hypostasis/subsistence of the Logos is communicated to Christ's flesh, two corollaries are drawn. First Ubiquitarians gather omnipresence and all properties of the Logos are communicated to the human nature — because the hypostasis of the Logos does not really differ from its essence nor from essential properties; if hypostasis is communicated, properties must be too. Second, some of our own theologians who think Christ's flesh can be said to subsist everywhere by the Logos's subsistence though it exists in one place alone argue: the Logos's subsistence is communicated to the human nature; that subsistence is infinite and bounded by no place; therefore the flesh can be said to subsist everywhere by that communicated subsistence. This latter argument is more dangerous than the former because it so pleases some Orthodox theologians that they profess we differ from Ubiquitarians in the controversy on local presence of Christ's flesh only by logomachia and verbal disagreement — let those who have carefully considered the history of the Mompelgart colloquy and the polemical writings of Beza and Jacob Andreae on this matter judge whether that is true. Para2 To dissolve those two arguments clearly, distinguish the verb 'to communicate' and teach in what sense Christ's subsistence is communicated to the flesh. Something is said to be communicated to another in three ways. First both inhesively and denominatively — as the odor of an apple is communicated to the hand: the odor (at least the same in kind) inheres in the hand and denominates it, i.e. is truly predicated of the hand. Second denominatively but not inhesively — as kings and emperors communicate imperial dignity to their wives, who are called Empresses and queens not because they have imperial power in themselves but because their husbands have that authority. Third neither inhesively nor denominatively but either effectively — as God is said to communicate himself to created beings, which are called beings and goods by participation of the first being and first good, as Zanchius speaks — or sustentatively — as the subject is communicated to its accidents by sustaining and receiving them in itself — or some similar mode. These are neither denominative nor inhesive communications because God neither exists in creatures as essential or accidental form in its subject nor is predicated of them by true affirmative predication; and the subject neither inheres in its accidents nor denominates them but is rather denominated by them. Para3 The hypostasis or subsistence of the Logos is communicated to his human nature in this third mode: neither inhesively nor denominatively but sustentatively only. Prior part of the assertion: Christ's human nature (as Martinius well notes against Menzer) is void of all proper personal subsistence and in no way subsists — neither per se nor by accident; more plainly, neither by its own nature nor from the union. Therefore the Logos's subsistence is not communicated to it inhesively or denominatively. Proof of antecedent: if Christ's humanity somehow subsists it is somehow a suppositum or person, and so in some sense it would be true that Christ assumed a suppositum or person — which is absurd. Proof of the connected claim: suppositum and subsistence reciprocate — every suppositum has subsistence and everything having subsistence is a suppositum. Objection: then Christ's flesh is plainly stripped of personality. Answer: it is not stripped in the sense of not being united to some person — it is united to the person of the Logos — but properly and formally subsistence neither inheres in it nor can be attributed to it. Para4 Same demonstrated another way: if Christ's human nature subsists, either it subsists per se (has subsistence from itself) or it subsists insofar as it exists in the person of the Logos. Former admitted by none; latter not free of clear absurdity. Proof: Christ's flesh insofar as it exists in the person of the Logos has a mode of existing contrary to subsistence; therefore it does not subsist. Antecedent: to be in another suppositum and to subsist (to be per se and outside every other suppositum) are two opposite modes of existing; flesh existing in the Logos's person has the former mode (exists in a suppositum) and therefore cannot have the latter, which is diametrically opposed. Para5 Posterior part of the assertion: the Logos graciously received and assumed our nature to his hypostasis so that his hypostasis has the flesh intimately present to itself and bears it personally united; conversely the flesh clings in that hypostasis and is sustained. Hence Christ's hypostasis or personal subsistence is rightly said to be communicated to the human nature sustentatively. Para6 From this distinction of communication it is clear what to answer to both arguments proposed at the article's threshold. Since Christ's hypostasis is communicated to his humanity neither inhesively nor denominatively, Ubiquitarians cannot gather from communication of the Logos's hypostasis that essential properties were communicated to the assumed flesh inhesively or denominatively — deny all those inferences concluding the flesh is omniscient, omnipresent, omnipotent, etc. Likewise, since all those statements attributing to Christ's flesh to subsist or to have some personal being are false — because it has no subsistence proper to itself, no personal being, but a mode of existing contrary to them — it follows that Christ's humanity can neither be said to subsist everywhere by the Logos's subsistence nor to exist everywhere according to its personal being. Objection: human nature is joined to the person of the Logos who is omnipresent and omnipotent; therefore human nature can be called omnipresent and omnipotent personally. Reply: if that consequence is admitted, equally these must be: human nature united to an infinite and eternal person is therefore itself infinite and eternal personally / according to its personal being; likewise joined to the person who is God and Creator and redeemer of the world, therefore these belong to it personally. Para7 Someone will ask whether as the act of subsisting so also the act of existing is to be removed from Christ's flesh. Reply: by no means — though the flesh does not subsist, it truly has its own existence distinct from the Logos's existence but dependent on it. Distinct because every created being has essence and existence distinct from the creator's; dependent because it cannot exist per se and outside the person of the Logos.
pass_b_english: Article XII. Whether the personal subsistence of the Logos is communicated to his human nature; and whether they speak rightly who say Christ's humanity subsists everywhere by that subsistence.

1. From the common saying that the hypostasis, or subsistence, of the Logos is communicated to Christ's flesh, two corollaries are drawn. First, the Ubiquitarians gather from it that omnipresence — indeed all the properties of the Logos — are communicated to the human nature. The reason of the consequence is that the hypostasis of the Logos does not really differ from its essence, and therefore not from its essential properties either: if therefore it is true that the hypostasis of the Logos is communicated to the flesh, it must also be granted that his properties are communicated to it in the same way. Second, some even among our own theologians, who think Christ's flesh can be said to subsist in every place by the subsistence of the Logos although it exists in one place alone, reason from the same foundation thus: the subsistence of the Logos is communicated to Christ's human nature; since therefore the subsistence of the Logos is infinite and is enclosed by the bounds of no place, Christ's flesh, by that subsistence communicated to it, can be said to subsist everywhere. This latter argument is more dangerous than the former, because it so greatly pleases certain Orthodox theologians that they profess that in this controversy concerning the local presence of Christ's flesh we differ from the Ubiquitarians only by a dispute about words, and by a merely verbal disagreement — which, whether it be true, let those judge who have more carefully considered the history of the colloquy of Mompelgart and the polemical writings of Beza and of Jacob Andreae on this matter.

2. In order, then, that those two arguments may be clearly dissolved, the verb 'to communicate' must be distinguished, and it must be taught in what sense Christ's subsistence is communicated to the flesh. It is therefore to be held that something is said to be communicated to another in three ways. First, both inhesively and denominatively, in the way the odor of an apple is communicated to the hand; for that odor, at least the same in kind, inheres in the hand and denominates the hand — that is, is truly predicated of the hand. Second, something is communicated denominatively but not inhesively: in the way kings and emperors communicate the dignity of empire to their wives; for those wives are denominated Empresses and queens, not because they have imperial power or authority in themselves, but because their husbands have that authority. Third, something is communicated to another neither inhesively nor denominatively, but either effectively — in the way God is said to communicate himself to created beings, for those beings are called beings and goods by participation of the first being and the first good, as Zanchius speaks — or sustentatively, in the way a subject is communicated to its accidents, namely by sustaining them and receiving them into itself; or in some other similar mode. I say these are communicated neither denominatively nor inhesively, because God neither exists in creatures as an essential form, or as an accidental form in its subject, nor is predicated of them by true and affirmative predication; and the subject likewise neither inheres in its accidents nor denominates them, but on the contrary is denominated by them.

3. The hypostasis or subsistence of the Logos is communicated to his human nature in this third way: that is, it is communicated to it neither inhesively nor denominatively, but sustentatively only. The prior part of this assertion is declared thus: Christ's human nature (as Martinius well notes against Menzer) is void of all proper personal subsistence, and in no way subsists — that is, neither by itself nor by accident; or, to speak more plainly, neither by its own nature nor from the union. Therefore the subsistence of the Logos is communicated to it neither inhesively nor denominatively. The antecedent is proved: if Christ's humanity somehow subsists, it is somehow a suppositum or person, and therefore in some sense it will be true that Christ assumed a suppositum or a person; but the latter is absurd; therefore the former also. The connected claim is proved, because suppositum and subsistence reciprocate, so that every suppositum has subsistence, and everything that has subsistence is a suppositum. Someone will say: therefore Christ's flesh is plainly stripped of personality. It is answered that it is not stripped of personality in this sense, as if it were not united to some person — for it is united to the person of the Logos — but that subsistence properly and formally neither inheres in it nor can be attributed to it.

4. The same can also be demonstrated thus: if Christ's human nature subsists, either it subsists by itself — that is, has subsistence from itself — or it subsists insofar as it exists in the person of the Logos. The former will be admitted by no one; but neither is the latter free of manifest absurdity. Which is proved thus: Christ's flesh, insofar as it exists in the person of the Logos, has a certain mode of existing contrary to subsistence; therefore it does not subsist. The antecedent is proved: to be in another suppositum, and to subsist — that is, to be by oneself and outside every other suppositum — are two opposite modes of existing; but Christ's flesh, insofar as it exists in the person of the Logos, has the former mode of existing, that is, it exists in a suppositum; therefore it cannot have the latter, which is diametrically opposed to it.

5. The posterior part of our assertion is declared thus: the Logos graciously received and assumed our nature to his hypostasis, so that his hypostasis has the flesh intimately present to itself and bears it personally united to itself; but on the contrary the flesh clings in that hypostasis and is sustained. From which it follows that Christ's hypostasis, or personal subsistence, is rightly said to be communicated to the human nature sustentatively.

6. From this distinction of communication it is clear what is to be answered to either argument proposed at the threshold of this article. For since Christ's hypostasis is communicated to his humanity neither inhesively nor denominatively, it is evident that the Ubiquitarians cannot gather from the communication of the hypostasis of the Logos that his essential properties have been communicated to the assumed flesh, either inhesively or denominatively; and therefore all those inferences are to be denied by which, from that foundation, they conclude that Christ's flesh is omniscient, omnipresent, omnipotent, and so on. Likewise, since all those statements are false by which to subsist, or to have some personal being, is attributed to Christ's flesh — because, namely, it has no subsistence proper to itself, and no personal being, but a certain mode of existing contrary to them — it follows that Christ's humanity can neither be said to subsist everywhere by the subsistence of the Logos, nor to exist everywhere according to its personal being. Someone will say: Christ's human nature is joined to the person of the Logos, who is omnipresent and omnipotent; therefore the human nature can be called omnipresent and omnipotent personally. Answer: if that consequence is admitted, by equal reason these consequences also must be admitted: Christ's human nature is united to an infinite and eternal person; therefore it itself is infinite and eternal personally, or according to its personal being. Likewise, it is joined to that person who is God and Creator, and redeemer of the world; therefore these things belong to it personally.

7. Someone will ask here whether, just as the act of subsisting, so also the act of existing is to be removed from Christ's flesh. Answer: by no means. For Christ's flesh, although it does not subsist, nevertheless in truth has its own existence, distinct from the existence of the Logos, but dependent upon it. I say that it has an existence distinct from the existence of the Logos, because every created being has both an essence and an existence distinct from the essence and existence of the creator. I say that it has an existence depending on the existence of the Logos, because it cannot exist by itself and outside the person of the Logos.
source_text:
ART. XII.
An subsistentia personalis τοῦ Λόγου, sit naturae ejus humanae communicata: Et an recte loquantur, qui dicunt, humanitatem CHRISTI subsistere ubique, per subsistentiam τοῦ Λόγου; Item existere ubique secundum esse suum personale.

1. Ex eo quod dici solet hypostasin, aut subsistentiam τοῦ Λόγου, communicatam esse carni CHRISTI, duo consectaria dicuntur: primo enim Ubiquitarii inde colligunt, omnipraesentiam, imo & proprietates omnes τοῦ Λόγου, esse humanae naturae communicatas; ratio consequentiae est, quia hypostasis τοῦ Λόγου non differt realiter ab ejus essentia; ideoque nec a proprietatibus ejus essentialibus: Si igitur verum est hypostasin τοῦ Λόγου, esse carni communicatam, etiam proprietates ejus, eodem modo ei communicatas esse fatendum est. Secundo, nonnulli etiam ex nostris Theologis, qui putant CHRISTI carnem posse dici ubique locorum subsistere, per subsistentiam τοῦ Λόγου, licet in uno solo existat, ex eodem fundamento, sic ratiocinantur, Humanae naturae CHRISTI communicata est subsistentia τοῦ Λόγου; cum igitur τοῦ Λόγου subsistentia infinita sit, & nullius loci ambitu includatur, caro CHRISTI, per eam subsistentiam sibi communicatam, dici potest ubique subsistere: hoc posterius argumentum periculosius est praecedente, quia tantopere placet quibusdam Orthodoxis Theologis, ut profiteantur nos in hac controversia de locali praesentia carnis CHRISTI, λογομαχίᾳ, & nonnisi verbali dissidio, ab Ubiquitariis discrepare; quod an verum sit, judicent illi qui historiam colloquii Mompelgartensis & Bezae ac Jacobi Andreae Polemica scripta super hac materia diligentius considerarunt.

2. Ut igitur duo illa argumenta perspicue diluantur, distinguendum est verbum communicandi, & docendum quo sensu CHRISTI subsistentia sit carni communicata: tenendum igitur est, aliquid tribus modis dici alteri communicari. Primo, & inhaesive & denominative, quo modo odor pomi communicatur manui, nam & odor ille, saltem idem specie, inest manui, & denominat manum, i. e. vere praedicatur de manu. Secundo, communicatur aliquid denominative, sed non inhaesive: quo pacto reges & imperatores communicant imperii dignitatem uxoribus suis, illae enim denominantur Imperatrices, & reginae, non quod in se habeant potestatem, aut authoritatem imperialem, sed quod earum mariti istam authoritatem habeant. Tertio, communicatur aliquid alteri, neque inhaesive, neque denominative, sed vel effective, quo modo DEUS dicitur communicare seipsum creatis entibus; illa enim dicuntur entia & bona, participatione primi entis, & primi boni, ut loquitur Zanchius; vel sustentative, quo modo accidentibus suis communicatur subjectum, ea videlicet sustentando, et recipiendo in se: vel aliquo alio simili modo. Dico haec neque communicari denominative, neque inhaesive, quia DEUS neque existit in creaturis tanquam forma essentialis, aut accidentalis in suo subjecto: neque de iis praedicatur, praedicatione vera & affirmativa: subjectum etiam neque inest accidentibus suis, neque ea denominat, sed contra ab iis denominatur.

3. Hypostasis seu subsistentia τοῦ Λόγου, tertio hoc modo communicatur naturae ejus humanae: h. e. neque communicatur ei inhaesive, neque denominative, sed sustentative tantum. Prior pars hujus assertionis sic declaratur: Humana natura CHRISTI (ut bene notat Martinius contra Menzerum.) omnis propriae personalis subsistentiae expers est, & nullo modo subsistit; h. e. neque per se, neque per accidens; sive, ut planius loquar, neque natura sua, neque ex unione. Ergo subsistentia τοῦ Λόγου, neque inhaesive, neque denominative ei communicata est: Probatur antecedens: Si humanitas CHRISTI aliquo modo subsistit, aliquo modo est suppositum aut persona, & proinde aliquo sensu verum erit, CHRISTUM assumpsisse suppositum, aut personam: at absurdum est posterius; Ergo etiam prius. Probatur connexum, quia suppositum & subsistentia reciprocantur, adeo ut omne suppositum habeat subsistentiam, & omne subsistentiam habens sit suppositum. Dicet aliquis: Ergo caro CHRISTI plane destituitur personalitate. Respondetur, eam non destitui personalitate hoc sensu, quasi non sit personae alicui unita, est enim unita personae τοῦ Λόγου; sed quod subsistentia proprie, & formaliter ei neque insit, neque attribui possit.

4. Idem etiam sic demonstrari potest: Si humana natura CHRISTI subsistit, vel per se subsistit, id est, ex se subsistentiam habet, vel subsistit quatenus existit in persona τοῦ Λόγου: prius a nullo admittetur: at neque posterius manifesta absurditate caret: quod sic probatur: Caro CHRISTI, quatenus existit in persona τοῦ Λόγου, habet modum quendam existendi subsistentiae contrarium, Ergo non subsistit. Probatur antecedens: Esse in alio supposito, & subsistere, seu esse per se, & extra omne aliud suppositum, sunt duo oppositi modi existendi, at caro CHRISTI, quatenus existit in persona τοῦ Λόγου, habet priorem modum existendi, i. e. existit in supposito: Ergo non potest habere posteriorem, qui ei e diametro opponitur.

5. Posterior pars nostrae assertionis sic declaratur: ὁ Λόγος naturam nostram, ad suam hypostasin gratiose recepit & assumpsit, ita ut ejus hypostasis carnem sibi intime praesentem habeat, eamque sibi personaliter unitam gestet: contra vero caro in illa hypostasi haereat, & sustentetur. Ex quo fit, ut CHRISTI hypostasis, seu personalis subsistentia, recte dicatur communicata humanae naturae sustentative.

6. Ex hac distinctione communicationis liquet, quid respondendum sit ad utrumque argumentum, in limine hujus articuli propositum: cum enim hypostasis CHRISTI neque inhaesive, neque denominative communicata sit humanitati ipsius; evidens est Ubiquitarios, ex communicatione hypostaseos τοῦ Λόγου, non posse colligere, proprietates ejus essentiales communicatas esse assumptae carni, aut inhaesive, aut denominative; & proinde negandas esse omnes illas illationes, quibus ex eo fundamento concludunt carnem CHRISTI esse omniscientem, omnipraesentem, omnipotentem, &c. Similiter, cum falsae sint omnes illae enuntiationes, quibus subsistere, aut esse aliquod personale carni CHRISTI tribuitur, quia viz. nullam habet subsistentiam sibi convenientem, nullumque esse personale, sed modum quendam existendi iis contrarium, consequens est CHRISTI humanitatem, neque posse dici subsistere ubique per subsistentiam τοῦ Λόγου, neque existere ubique secundum esse suum personale. Dicet aliquis, natura humana CHRISTI conjuncta est cum persona τοῦ Λόγου, quae omnipraesens est, & omnipotens: Ergo natura humana dici potest omnipraesens, & omnipotens personaliter. Resp. Si ista consequentia admittatur, pari ratione admittendae etiam sunt hae consequentiae: Humana natura CHRISTI unita est cum persona infinita, & aeterna: Ergo ipsa est infinita & aeterna personaliter, seu secundum suum esse personale: Item, est conjuncta cum ea persona, quae DEUS est & Creator, ac redemptor Mundi: Ergo haec ei conveniunt personaliter.

7. Quaeret hic aliquis, an quemadmodum actus subsistendi, ita etiam actus existendi, a CHRISTI carne removendus sit. Resp. Nequaquam: caro enim CHRISTI, licet non subsistat, revera tamen habet propriam existentiam, distinctam ab existentia τοῦ Λόγου, sed ab ea dependentem. Dico eam habere existentiam distinctam ab existentia τοῦ Λόγου, quia omne Ens creatum habet & essentiam, & existentiam distinctam ab essentia & existentia creatoris. Dico eam habere existentiam pendentem ab existentia τοῦ Λόγου, quia per se, & extra personam τοῦ Λόγου, existere non potest.
